# The Generalist Is Back. They Just Used to Be a Specialist


Written By aryan.ahmed@hackerrank.com | November 23, 2026


“A jack of all trades is master of none.”


It is


*the* line people reach for when someone can’t seem to pick a lane. It’s the person who touches front-end, infra, and data but isn’t particularly great enough at any of those tasks to be the first pick for a project. The generalist.


At some point, the internet added a second phrase: “but oftentimes better than a master of one.” A redemption, of sorts, for Jack. Which is, more or less, what’s happening to the generalist right now.


A major sign: LinkedIn has ended its associate product manager programme. In its place, there is an “Associate Product Builder” track and a formal “Full Stack Builder” title. Applicants send a working product instead of a résumé.


For two decades, tech hired for the first half of the proverb. Front-end developers, back-end developers, DevOps engineers, data engineers, ML engineers: every new layer of software got its own specialist, and every specialist got a narrower job title.


But the trend is shifting. As PwC said in its 2026 predictions: “AI could soon end a shift that has marked most of the industrial era – the ever-increasing specialization of work.”


## **The full-stack era**


When Anthropic surveyed 132 of its own engineers and researchers in 2025, one finding stood out: everyone was becoming more ‘full-stack’. Security teams were using Claude to make sense of code they didn’t know. The alignment team was building front-end visualisations. One engineer said, “I can very capably work on front-end, or transactional databases, or API code.”


These were people who would once have handed that work to someone else. Run off to the security team, or IT, or design. Now they didn’t have to.


A field experiment at Procter & Gamble found the same thing outside software. Researchers from Harvard and Wharton gave 776 P&G professionals real product problems to solve. With AI, one person working alone did as well as a two-person team without it. Without AI, R&D staff pitched technical ideas and commercial staff pitched commercial ones. With AI, both came up with balanced solutions.


The job market is following. Forward deployed engineers, who write production code inside a customer’s business and spend as much time understanding the client’s problem as building the fix, are among the fastest-growing roles in tech. According to Indeed, job postings for them in India grew nearly 19-fold between June 2025 and June 2026. GTM engineers, who wire up sales and marketing systems with code, saw postings grow 205% year-on-year.


Neither job fits neatly into one box anymore. AI has transformed them all. More and more jobs now ask people to both write code and understand the business it’s for. An engineer might spend the morning learning how a customer’s team works and the afternoon building something to help it. So the skill being hired for is judgment across domains: knowing which code a business needs, and why. Something a generalist might know.


But here’s the catch. The generalists winning right now didn’t start out as they are today.


PwC, which calls this the “rise of the AI generalist,” says so itself. “One experienced software engineer can orchestrate teams of AI agents at work in many or even all stages,” its report on agentic workforces said. The engineer can do it because they have built software the hard way before. “The new generalists don’t build themselves,” PwC said.


In a July 2025 Fastly survey of 791 developers, about a third of senior developers, those with 10 or more years of experience, said more than half the code they ship is AI-generated. Among juniors, it was 13%. Seniors also said they spend more time fixing what the AI writes. They have the experience to tell when it’s wrong.


And that ability to tell is the whole game. Anthropic called it the paradox of supervision: checking an AI’s work takes exactly the coding skills that leaning on AI wears down. “I am for sure atrophying in my skills as a software engineer,” one engineer said.


So is the master of one obsolete? Hardly. The master of one is now becoming a jack of all trades.


## **The future**


In May 2026, HackerRank ran Orchestrate, a 24-hour hackathon where 12,885 registrants set out to build an AI agent from scratch. Submissions were scored four ways: code quality, accuracy, the candidate’s chat history with the AI, and a 30-minute interview about the build. Every one of the top 10 finished in the top quarter on all four.


The best builders used AI as a tool. They made a plan before they started, checked the AI’s work against real data, and stayed in charge of every decision. The weaker candidates let the AI drive.


That’s what a good builder looks like today. The harder question is where the next ones come from. If today’s best generalists are yesterday’s specialists, who trains the next batch?


The early data says less about whether juniors get hired than about what AI is doing in their jobs. Researchers at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab, using payroll data, found that employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in the jobs most exposed to AI is 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with less-exposed fields. But the drop is concentrated in jobs where AI does the work instead of people. Where AI mostly helps people do their work, employment is flat or rising, especially for more experienced workers.


Juniors are still being hired. HackerRank’s own 2025 Developer Skills Report found entry-level hiring rose 7% year-on-year in 2024. What’s changed is what they’re hired for. AI is reshaping what junior developers are responsible for.


Whether those juniors grow into tomorrow’s generalists depends largely on how they use AI, the same thing that separated the best builders at Orchestrate. In a January 2026 experiment, Anthropic had 52 mostly junior engineers learn a new Python library. Those who used AI to ask questions and understand the code averaged 65% or higher on a quiz afterwards. Those who handed the whole job over to the AI averaged below 40%.


The proverb got its kinder ending eventually. Jack might be getting one too. For years, the only way to tell if someone had good judgment was to count their years in one lane, which is why the specialist got picked first. Now judgment shows up in how someone works: what they plan, what they question, when they take the wheel back from the AI. The generalist – and their AI – may have a fair shot.
